Accessibility

Every park says what is actually accessible.

Not a compliance badge in the footer. Parking, paved route, restroom and playground surfacing are stated on the park card and the park page, because the people who need that information are looking for it before they leave the house.

Foundation for
Centerville-Washington ParksA separate 501(c)(3)

Different organization, different front door.

The Foundation raises the money the tax levy does not cover. It gets its own section on foundation.cwpd.org with its own identity — different mark, different typography, different colour — so a donation is never mistaken for a program fee.

What this concept demonstrates

Six decisions, each tied to something in your RFP.

01

Results that answer the question

Your RFP asks that search results give enough information to judge a park without opening every page. Amenities, accessibility, trail mileage and distance live on the card itself.

02

Tasks before storytelling

Field status and Find a Park are your two most visited pages after the home page. They appear in the first screen on a phone, in a row of verbs rather than a menu of departments.

03

Accessibility as information

Every park states what is actually accessible: parking, paved route, restroom, playground surfacing. Your senior audience comes to the site for exactly that.

04

RecDesk without double entry

Programs reach the park page, the listings and search from one synced source. Full and cancelled sessions drop out on their own wherever the API allows it.

05

Alerts that people read

A single banner directly under the header, with the affected park named and a link to the full status. It never competes with the hero for attention.

06

Your identity, not ours

Tree mark, woodland palette and your own tagline. Final colour and type follow the brand guide you provide at kickoff; this concept commits to structure and behaviour.

Stay in the loop

Monthly news, program announcements and park project updates.
